A.explanation: Symmetrical triangular waves imply equal time in the air and in contact with equal magnitudes of acceleration, but contact time is very short with very large upward acceleration.

B.explanation: A continuous sine wave implies simple harmonic motion with continuously varying acceleration, but the girl is mostly in free fall with constant acceleration $-g$.

C.explanation: The curved sections during flight are wrong because free fall has constant acceleration so the $v$-$t$ graph must be straight lines of constant negative gradient.

D.explanation: Long straight sections of constant negative slope show free fall under $g$, interrupted by short steep positive slopes showing the large upward acceleration during trampoline contact.

hints: Notice how the motion divides into a long time airborne and a very short time in contact with the trampoline.
Recall that in the air acceleration is almost constant at $-g$, so the $v$-$t$ gradient $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$ must be constant and negative - a straight falling line.
Look for the graph with long straight falls through $v=0$ plus a brief very steep rise from negative to positive $v$ for the bounce.
walkthrough: Start with the airborne phase: after leaving the trampoline the girl is in free fall, so acceleration $a = -g$ is constant if upward $v$ is positive.

For constant $a$, velocity obeys $v = u + at$, so the $v$-$t$ graph is a straight line with constant negative gradient $-g$ while she rises, stops instantaneously at $v=0$, then falls to negative $v$.
On hitting the trampoline she is rapidly decelerated downward and accelerated upward, so velocity must change from a large negative value to a large positive value in a very short time $\Delta t$.
That bounce therefore appears as a short section with a very large positive gradient, much steeper than the $-g$ slope in the air.
Only the graph with repeating long straight-line falls interrupted by brief steep rises matches this, with sharp turnarounds at the top where $v$ crosses zero linearly. This is option D
